whyCorrect: The text sets up a problem and then hands you the fix. The problem: reading the piece as being about constraints on women leaves Sandoval, a man taped to the same wall, unexplained. The fix is the 1974 context — the art establishment recognized only sociohistorical muralists, so every nonmuralist Chicano artist, male or female, was boxed in by aesthetic expectations. A conclusion that "accounts for all the evidence" has to cover both artists, and only the reading about Chicano artists in general does that.

whyWrong.A: Splits the work into two separate meanings, one per artist, when the text asks for a single interpretation that accounts for all the evidence; it also assigns frustration to muralists, who were the group the establishment did recognize.
whyWrong.B: Keeps women at the center, which is exactly the reading the text says fails because it cannot explain Sandoval.
whyWrong.C: Turns the muralists themselves into the target. The text criticizes the establishment for recognizing only muralists, never the content of what muralists depicted.

commonMistakes: Choosing the option that sounds most sophisticated instead of the one that resolves the specific gap the text identifies.
tips: When a text names an unexplained detail, the correct completion is the one that explains that detail.

whyCorrect: Neither noun owns anything here. You place your hands (more than one hand, plain plural) between the two antennas (plain plural, and "two" already tells you it is plural). Nothing belongs to the hands and nothing belongs to the antennas, so no apostrophe is needed anywhere.

whyWrong.A: Uses the singular "hand's" after "your ... two antennas" implies both hands, and adds a possessive apostrophe to "antenna's" where the sentence needs the plain plural "antennas."
whyWrong.C: Marks both nouns as possessive. Ask what the hands own and what the antennas own — the sentence never says, which is the signal that no apostrophe belongs.
whyWrong.D: Correctly leaves "antennas" plain but still makes "hands'" possessive; the hands do not own the space between the antennas, they are simply placed there.

tips: Before writing an apostrophe, finish the phrase "the ___ of the ___." If it makes no sense, you need a plain plural.

whyCorrect: The blank sits inside a three-item list of past participles: the sculptures had been cut, bent, and welded. A list of three takes a comma after each of the first two items and nothing after the conjunction, so the punctuation you need is "cut, bent, and" followed directly by "welded."

whyWrong.A: Adds a comma after "and," which separates the conjunction from the item it introduces; nothing ever goes between "and" and the last list item.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon separates full clauses or items that already contain commas. "Cut" and "bent" are single words, so a semicolon is far too heavy here.
whyWrong.D: Drops the comma after "cut," leaving the first two items run together as "cut bent" instead of as separate list items.

tips: Count the list items first; three parallel items means two commas and no punctuation after the conjunction.

whyCorrect: Strip the modifier and the subject is plain: "the toxins ... increase its attractiveness." Everything between "toxins" and the blank — "the organism uses to protect itself from predation" — is a relative clause describing the toxins, not a new subject. A plural subject in the present tense takes the base form "increase."

whyWrong.A: "Is" agrees with a singular subject, and the progressive also implies an action in progress rather than the general fact the sentence states.
whyWrong.C: Singular verb form. It sounds right only if you let "predation" or "the organism," the nearest nouns to the blank, act as the subject.
whyWrong.D: Singular, and the present perfect frames this as something that has happened rather than as a standing property of the toxins.

commonMistakes: Agreeing the verb with whichever noun sits closest to the blank instead of with the real subject.

whyCorrect: Two things have to happen at the blank. "Respectively" belongs to the main sentence — it tells you which molar mass goes with which compound — so it stays outside the parentheses and is set off by a comma. Then the whole side note about stoichiometry opens with the parenthesis, giving "g/mol, respectively (in stoichiometry, molar mass helps convert ...)."

whyWrong.A: Pulls "respectively" inside the parentheses, so the main sentence loses the word that pairs each number with its compound and the aside becomes two unrelated statements jammed together.
whyWrong.B: Places a comma immediately before an opening parenthesis. Punctuation never goes directly in front of "("; if a mark is needed there, it goes after the closing parenthesis.
whyWrong.C: Ends the sentence at "g/mol" and starts a new one with "Respectively," which now modifies nothing, and it opens the parenthesis in the middle of the aside so the parenthetical no longer contains a complete thought.

tips: Decide what belongs inside the parentheses before you decide where the commas go.

whyCorrect: Test both sides of the blank on their own. "Cut, bent, and welded ... the sculptures ... are meant to challenge viewers to consider their own relationships to material wastes" is a complete sentence, and "her thought-provoking works in the 1999 exhibition ... were no different" is also a complete sentence. Two independent clauses joined with no coordinating conjunction require a semicolon.

whyWrong.B: "And to" tries to extend the earlier list, producing "relationships to material wastes and to her thought-provoking works ... were no different," which leaves the second clause with no grammatical home.
whyWrong.C: A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a comma splice.
whyWrong.D: No punctuation at all fuses the two clauses into a run-on.

commonMistakes: Assuming the second half continues the first because it starts with "her"; check whether it has its own subject and verb, and here it does.

whyCorrect: The subject of the blank is the gerund phrase "Distinguishing 'exactly the same' and 'nearly the same' commodities," and a gerund phrase is always singular no matter how many nouns sit inside it. The dashes fence off "whether crops, lumber, or precious metals" as an interruption, so it cannot supply the subject. Singular subject, past tense: "was."

whyWrong.A: Plural verb, chosen by agreeing with the plural nouns "commodities" or "metals" instead of with the gerund phrase that heads the subject.
whyWrong.C: "Having been" is a participle, not a finite verb, so the sentence never gets a main verb and stays a fragment.
whyWrong.D: "Being" is likewise nonfinite and leaves the sentence with no predicate.

tips: Cross out anything between a pair of dashes before deciding what the subject is.

whyCorrect: The first sentence makes a claim — the upward trend in urbanization held "throughout that part of the continent" — and the second sentence backs it with the region-wide figures, 44.5% to 47.7% over the same years. That is confirmation of the claim just made, which is what "Indeed" signals.

whyWrong.A: "Nevertheless" announces a contrast, but the regional numbers rise just as Burkina's do, so there is nothing to contrast.
whyWrong.B: "Later" marks a shift forward in time, yet both sentences cover the identical 2015-2020 window.
whyWrong.D: "In reality" corrects a mistaken impression; the second sentence confirms the first rather than correcting it.

commonMistakes: Reading two different sets of percentages as a contrast when they actually move in the same direction.

whyCorrect: The colon sets up what follows as the outcome of the plant pulling iron out of the ground and locking it into its roots and shoots. If the iron ends up inside the plant, the soil necessarily has less of it. The blank needs a cause-and-effect signal, and "accordingly" is the one that says "as a result of what was just described."

whyWrong.A: "Specifically" promises a narrower restatement of the previous idea, but soil concentrations dropping is a new consequence, not a detail of how the plant stores iron.
whyWrong.B: "Nevertheless" sets up a contrast; falling soil iron agrees with the storage described before it, so there is nothing to contrast.
whyWrong.C: "In addition" makes the two facts parallel and independent, hiding the fact that one causes the other.

tips: Ask whether the second idea follows from the first or merely sits beside it; only the first case takes a result transition.

whyCorrect: The first sentence establishes when these amphibians migrate: during the day, unlike most animals. The second sentence explains what happens in that daytime window — the sun is up, so predators that hunt by sight can see the warning colors. The blank has to point back to that time period, which is what "At that time" does.

whyWrong.B: "For example" would require the second sentence to be an instance of the claim before it, but it gives the reason daytime migration is safe rather than an example of it.
whyWrong.C: "In other words" signals a restatement, and the second sentence adds new information about color patterns and predator vision.
whyWrong.D: "However" signals contrast, yet the second sentence supports the first by explaining how the amphibians stay safe.

commonMistakes: Reaching for a contrast word because the first sentence starts with "While"; that contrast is already handled inside the sentence itself.

whyCorrect: The goal names one thing: the role Morris played. His role is keyboardist, and the notes add that he was one of the musicians invited to tour. Choice A puts both in the predicate — "performed with OTS as a touring keyboardist" — so the sentence lands on what he did rather than on when he did it.

whyWrong.B: Uses Morris only as one end of a range of guest musicians, so the emphasis falls on the band's practice of inviting performers, not on his role.
whyWrong.C: Says only that he toured, which leaves out the keyboardist role entirely.
whyWrong.D: The "It was in 2000 that ..." construction is a cleft that puts the stress on the year; the role is mentioned but demoted to a modifier.

tips: When a stem says "emphasize X," check which part of the sentence X occupies — emphasis lives in the main clause, not in a stray adjective.

whyCorrect: The goal is to name the specific type of neutrino research, and the notes give exactly one: neutrino oscillations. Only choice C both identifies Kim and states that his known research is on oscillations, so it is the only option that satisfies the stem's requirement.

whyWrong.A: Describes neutrinos in general and never mentions Kim or any research of his.
whyWrong.B: Gives his field and nationality, which is background, not the type of research.
whyWrong.D: Says he has advanced understanding of neutrinos but stops short of naming oscillations, so the specific type is still missing.

commonMistakes: Picking a sentence that is accurate and well written without checking that it contains the one detail the stem demands.

whyCorrect: A comparison has to state how the two hypotheses relate on the same measure. The notes give that measure: Fodor counts only low-level systems as modular, while Carruthers's MMH counts all cognitive systems. Choice B puts both on that scale and says Fodor's definition is the less expansive of the two, which is the comparison the student wants.

whyWrong.A: Misreports the disagreement. Both scientists accept that the mind contains innate modules; they differ over how far modularity extends.
whyWrong.C: Contradicts the notes. Both hypotheses treat low-level systems such as perception and language as modular, so that is where they agree, not where they differ.
whyWrong.D: Only puts the two in chronological order and describes Carruthers's view; Fodor's position is never characterized, so nothing is compared.

tips: For a comparison task, make sure the sentence says something about both items on a single shared dimension.

whyCorrect: The second sentence tells you what was missing before 1917: a procedure that senators could put into use to cut off debate and force a vote. The blank therefore needs a word meaning "called upon" or "put into effect," which is what it means to invoke a rule or measure.

whyWrong.A: "Improvised" means made up on the spot, which contradicts "formal measure" — a formal rule is exactly the thing you do not invent in the moment.
whyWrong.C: "Abolished" means done away with. Abolishing a measure would not end a debate, and the sentence says no such measure existed to begin with.
whyWrong.D: "Partitioned" means divided into parts, which does nothing to stop a prolonged debate.

tips: Rules, powers, and procedures are invoked; the verb has to fit the noun it acts on.

whyCorrect: The second sentence is the evidence, and it is all positive: critics called one film "galvanizing" and the other "exuberant." "For example" marks it as an illustration of how the films are regarded now, so the blank must describe a positive reception.

whyWrong.B: "Skeptically" implies doubt, the opposite of the praise the example supplies.
whyWrong.C: "Neutrally" means without a positive or negative slant, but the quoted praise is plainly enthusiastic.
whyWrong.D: "Strangely" describes an odd manner of judging rather than a favorable one, and nothing in the example is odd.

commonMistakes: Letting the opening "Whatever the general attitude ... when they were initially released" push you toward a negative word; that clause refuses to say what the early reception was.

whyCorrect: The sentence contrasts two styles. Realists aimed at accuracy about ordinary working people; the romantic paintings did the opposite, and the tail of the sentence tells you how — they hid every imperfection. A style that hides flaws and plays up beauty or heroism is overstating those qualities, so "exaggerate" is the word that completes the contrast.

whyWrong.B: "Correct" would mean fixing an error in the subjects' beauty or heroism, which is not something a painting does to a quality.
whyWrong.C: "Undermine" means weaken. Weakening a subject's beauty runs against "hiding all imperfection," which is flattery, not criticism.
whyWrong.D: "Mock" makes the romantic painters ridicule their subjects, but they idealized them.

tips: When a sentence sets up a contrast, use the half you already understand — here, accuracy — to fix the direction of the missing word.

whyCorrect: The blank has to explain why researchers struggle to study these cats. The earlier sentences say they live alone in out-of-the-way places like Mount Everest, so the obstacle is that their habitats sit far away from where people are. "Distant from large populations of humans" restates "out-of-the-way" in the terms the sentence needs.

whyWrong.A: "Drawn to" would put the cats near people, which would make them easier to observe, not harder.
whyWrong.B: "Full of" large human populations contradicts "live mostly alone in out-of-the-way parts of Asia."
whyWrong.D: "Responsible for" large human populations makes no sense as a property of a habitat and does nothing to explain the research difficulty.

tips: A because-clause has to supply a cause; test each option by asking whether it would actually make research hard.

whyCorrect: Everything before the last sentence is a catalog of things to look at: silvered moss hung like festoons, pungent pine cones, resplendent green, cypresses spread along the water, weeping willows. "This gorgeous display" gathers all of that into one word, so "display" means an impressive sight — a spectacle.

whyWrong.B: "Reproduction" means a copy of something else, but the scenery is the real thing, not an imitation.
whyWrong.C: "Pretentiousness" carries a sneer at false grandeur; the passage admires the landscape without any hint of criticism.
whyWrong.D: "Disguise" implies something is being concealed, and nothing in the description hides anything.

commonMistakes: Choosing a meaning the word can carry in other contexts instead of the one the surrounding sentences actually support.

whyCorrect: Track the three moves. First, historians of capitalism say little about precolonial African capitalism and so leave the impression that capitalism was imposed from outside. Second, Candido and others show features of capitalism were already there. Third, the last sentence explains the gap: those historians rely on archival longitudinal data, which precolonial Africa largely lacks. That is a misleading feature of their work, followed by an account of why it arises.

whyWrong.A: No disagreement over what counts as a feature of capitalism appears; both sides use the same features, such as private property in land.
whyWrong.C: The Africanist scholars' method is never described or judged; the method discussed is that of the historians of capitalism.
whyWrong.D: There is no debate over interpreting archival data. The point is that the archival data does not exist for much of precolonial Africa.

tips: When the final sentence begins "One reason for this," the text's purpose almost always includes explaining something, not just reporting it.

whyCorrect: The opening sentence sets up that admired figures back Crowley's writing, and the rest of the text delivers one such endorsement in detail: Bloom praises Little, Big for blending Schiller's naive and sentimental modes when Schiller treated them as alternatives. The Schiller material exists to explain what Bloom admires, so the text's job is to give the reason behind a critic's high opinion of a novel.

whyWrong.A: Nothing is said about what prompted Crowley to write anything; the focus is on how a critic responded.
whyWrong.C: Merrill is named once as a champion of Crowley's work, and none of his own writing is described, so no comparison takes place.
whyWrong.D: The text says the opposite — Little, Big shows a work can be both naive and sentimental rather than one or the other.

commonMistakes: Mistaking Schiller's two-category scheme for the text's own claim; the passage cites it only to show what Crowley's novel breaks.

whyCorrect: The text names two advantages and endorses both. Community science promotes engagement by showing the public what a scientist's day looks like, and it is effective because it multiplies the data collected, as the butterfly study shows. The main idea has to keep both benefits and treat both as real, which only one option does.

whyWrong.A: Reduces the whole text to a single study, misnames the researcher, and invents a reaction of surprise that the text never reports.
whyWrong.C: Adds a drawback about data accuracy that the text never raises; the text calls the data increase a strength.
whyWrong.D: Keeps the data benefit but denies the engagement benefit, which the text states outright.

tips: When a text lists two advantages, the main idea is the option that carries both without adding a qualification of its own.

whyCorrect: Her behavior is checking repeatedly whether the guests have gone. The text then supplies the reason: the parlor is her space for her little school, the salon leaves it out of order, and it has to become a classroom again the next morning. She is waiting on the room, not on the people in it.

whyWrong.A: Nothing indicates any opinion of the guests; the text never reports what she thinks of them or any attempt to persuade them.
whyWrong.C: The school already exists and is held in that parlor; there is no new school and no plan she wants supported.
whyWrong.D: No task elsewhere in the house is mentioned, and her concern is with the parlor itself, not with Salome's availability.

commonMistakes: Reading impatience as dislike of the guests when the passage ties it to a practical need for the room.

whyCorrect: Turn the hypothesis into a prediction first. Large vortices produce big pressure fluctuations at the snout of narrow- and intermediate-headed fish but only small ones for wide-headed fish, so if greater fluctuations mean better avoidance, intermediate-headed fish should hit large-vortex obstructions less often than wide-headed fish do. A finding that the two groups bumped into obstructions equally often removes exactly the difference the hypothesis predicts.

whyWrong.A: Gives a rate for wide-headed fish alone with nothing to compare it against, so "less than half" cannot show whether the predicted gap exists.
whyWrong.C: Wide-headed fish bumping more often than intermediate-headed fish is precisely what the hypothesis predicts, so this supports it.
whyWrong.D: Compares individuals within one head shape, which says nothing about the relationship between pressure fluctuations and avoidance across shapes.

tips: Before reading the choices, write down what the hypothesis predicts should differ; a challenge is the finding where that difference fails to appear.

whyCorrect: The student's word is "must" — IGF-1 variation is being treated as the explanation for size differences between breeds. To undermine that, you only need to show the gene is not working alone. If IGF-1 is one of several genes known to affect dog size, then the size variance cannot be attributed to IGF-1 variants by itself.

whyWrong.A: Limits the finding to dogs versus other species, but the student's claim is only about dog breeds, so this leaves it untouched.
whyWrong.C: Says most breeds carry different variants, which is consistent with the variants tracking size differences rather than against it.
whyWrong.D: States that IGF-1 variation does produce substantial size variance, which agrees with the student instead of undermining the conclusion.

commonMistakes: Looking for a statement that contradicts the study's data; here the flaw is in the student's leap to a sole cause, so the counter is any evidence of other causes.

whyCorrect: The claim is that time is conceptualized on egocentric axes — directions defined by where the speaker's own body is pointed, the way English front/back works. A group that gestures uphill for the future no matter which way the speaker is facing is using the landscape, not the body, as its reference frame. That is a non-egocentric system in a real culture, which is enough to break a claim of universality.

whyWrong.A: Shared grammatical structures say nothing about whether the spatial frame is anchored to the speaker.
whyWrong.C: Opposite directions for past and future is exactly what an egocentric front/back scheme produces, so this fits the claim rather than weakening it.
whyWrong.D: A difference in how many gestures are used is about frequency, not about which axis the gestures are organized around.

tips: To weaken a universal claim you need one genuine counterexample, so look for the option that describes a system built on a different principle, not just a different amount.

whyCorrect: Two ideas have to combine. Camacho and McLachlan say "invasive" and "native" describe temporary circumstances, and climate change can push species out of old ranges and open up new ones. Apply that to Wisconsin's label on the walnut twig beetle and the conclusion is about time: the label can be right today and stop being right later.

whyWrong.A: Invents a history in which the beetle already lived in Wisconsin and was driven out; the text never discusses the beetle's past range.
whyWrong.B: Singles out the beetle as the one case where the distinction fails now, but the text's point is that the labels are temporary in general, not that this one case is special today.
whyWrong.C: Depends on climate not changing, while the whole inference rests on climate change altering where species can live.

commonMistakes: Concluding the labels are useless; the text says they are temporary, which is a claim about durability, not validity.

whyCorrect: Malthus was an economist writing about human population outrunning food production. Darwin's fall 1838 entry ties the biological struggle for survival to that essay by labeling it "as inference from Malthus," and the notebook begun in October 1838 echoes it with "the grand crush of population." So by October 1838 at the latest, Darwin had taken an idea from economics and applied it to living species.

whyWrong.A: The text dates the notebooks to 1838 and gives 1858 only as the publication year of On the Origin of Species; nothing places any entry that late.
whyWrong.B: Reverses the direction of influence. Darwin drew on Malthus, not the other way around, and no observation of animals is credited to Malthus.
whyWrong.D: Malthus wrote about human populations and agriculture, so the biological principle was not already stated in the same terms, and no other economists are mentioned.

tips: When a text gives two dates, check whether the question hinges on which came first; here the October notebook fixes the latest possible date.

whyCorrect: Turner is one of nearly two thousand African Americans, so that noun is a plain plural. The relative clause "who won elections" describes them, and "elections" is also a plain plural — the elections do not own anything in this sentence. No apostrophe belongs anywhere in the blank.

whyWrong.A: Puts possessive apostrophes on both nouns; "Americans'" would have to own something, and it owns nothing here.
whyWrong.B: "Election's" is possessive, but the sentence never names anything belonging to an election.
whyWrong.C: "American's" is singular possessive, which clashes with "nearly two thousand" and again marks ownership that does not exist.

tips: Numbers like "two thousand" force a plural noun, so any singular possessive in the choices can go immediately.

whyCorrect: The subject is "The trailblazing accomplishments," which is plural. Everything after it — "of Goldin, winner of the 2023 Nobel Prize in Economics for her work on women in the labor force" — is prepositional and appositive material that cannot change the subject's number. A plural subject in the present tense takes "attest."

whyWrong.A: Singular verb, which agrees with "Goldin" rather than with "accomplishments."
whyWrong.C: Also singular, and the present perfect frames the attesting as completed rather than as a continuing fact.
whyWrong.D: Singular, and the progressive suggests an action currently in progress, which does not fit a general statement about what her accomplishments show.

commonMistakes: Letting the long modifier between the subject and the verb pull the verb into agreement with the nearest name.

whyCorrect: "Hungary and Ireland" identifies which of the thirty-eight member nations the two prices belong to, and "respectively" only works if those names sit tight against the figures they pair with. That makes the names an essential appositive, and an essential appositive takes no punctuation before it: "in fellow OECD nations Hungary and Ireland, respectively."

whyWrong.A: A comma turns the names into supplementary information, which reads as though the fellow OECD nations were only Hungary and Ireland when there are thirty-eight.
whyWrong.B: A colon presents what follows as a separate specification set off from the clause, again loosening a link the sentence needs to keep tight for "respectively" to work.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon has to join two independent clauses, and "Hungary and Ireland, respectively" is not a clause at all.

tips: A common noun followed directly by the names it refers to — "the poet Keats," "fellow OECD nations Hungary and Ireland" — takes no punctuation between them.

whyCorrect: Both sides of the blank are complete: "The mycorrhizal association ... is well documented" and "sharing nutrients via fungal hyphae and the host tree's roots, the organisms form a kind of social system ..." Two independent clauses need a real boundary, and the dash supplies one. The colon is ruled out by the end of the same sentence, which already uses one before "a community"; two colons in a single sentence leave the reader unable to tell which one governs.

whyWrong.A: No punctuation at all runs the two clauses together.
whyWrong.B: A second colon in a sentence that already ends with "... than plants: a community" makes the structure ambiguous, even though a colon would otherwise be defensible here.
whyWrong.D: A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a comma splice.

tips: Read to the end of the sentence before choosing a colon; a mark that is fine in isolation can collide with punctuation already there.

whyCorrect: "Because" starts a clause, and a clause needs a subject and a verb. The only option that supplies both is "they're" — that is, "because they are descendants of Proto-Kru." The pronoun is plural because it stands for the thirty-eight Kru languages.

whyWrong.A: "Its" is a possessive with no verb, leaving "because its descendants of Proto-Kru" without a predicate, and it is singular besides.
whyWrong.C: "Their" is also possessive and verbless, producing the same fragment even though the number is right.
whyWrong.D: "It's" does contain a verb, but the singular "it" cannot refer to thirty-eight languages that are themselves the descendants.

tips: After "because," check first that the option gives you a subject and a verb; only then worry about which pronoun.

whyCorrect: "Writers of other literary forms ... are less likely to be recognized beyond their nations' borders, but many are still well known" is a finished sentence, and "Malika Ouattara, for example, is a celebrated slam poet from Burkina Faso" is a second complete sentence that illustrates it. A colon is the mark that lets a complete statement introduce the example that backs it up.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation the two clauses fuse into a run-on.
whyWrong.B: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.D: "And" joining two independent clauses needs a comma before it, and the sentence already runs on "but," so stacking a second conjunction blurs which clauses are being contrasted.

tips: When the second half opens with "for example" and is itself a full sentence, a colon or a period is almost always what the item is testing.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank gives one reason Hilo soil suits the state: it is abundant there. The sentence after gives a second, separate reason: it supports agriculture and grows crops like ginger and taro. Two reasons stacked in the same direction call for an addition transition.

whyWrong.A: "Alternatively" offers a competing option instead of the one just given, but the agricultural role does not replace abundance as a reason.
whyWrong.B: "By contrast" needs an opposition, and both facts argue for the same conclusion.
whyWrong.C: "At that time" points back to a moment in time, and no time frame has been established.

tips: Ask whether the second sentence replaces, opposes, or joins the first; only the third case takes "additionally."

whyCorrect: The two sentences report opposite halves of the same finding: at lower elevations the snowpack peaked in early March, at higher elevations in mid-March. The blank sits right after "At higher elevations," which already signals the switch to the other group, so the transition has to mark that the second result differs from the first.

whyWrong.A: "In other words" introduces a restatement, but mid-March is a different date from early March, not the same fact reworded.
whyWrong.B: "For instance" would make higher elevations an example of the lower-elevation finding, when they are the contrasting case.
whyWrong.D: "In summary" signals a wrap-up of everything before it, and this sentence adds a new result instead.

commonMistakes: Assuming that because both sentences come from one study they must agree; a single study routinely reports contrasting results for different conditions.

whyCorrect: The first sentence describes a method: instead of each woman taking her own male pseudonym, Bradley and Cooper published everything under one shared name. The second sentence states what that method achieved — the expression of a joint creative vision. "In this way" is the transition that says the result came about by the means just described.

whyWrong.B: "For instance" makes the second sentence an example of the first, but it reports the outcome of the practice rather than an instance of it.
whyWrong.C: "Later" places the second sentence at a subsequent time, and the four decades of shared publication are the same period, not a later one.
whyWrong.D: "On the other hand" sets up a contrast, while the second sentence follows directly from the first.

tips: When one sentence describes how something was done and the next describes what it accomplished, the link is method-to-result.

whyCorrect: The stem asks for two things at once: a general claim about symbols on flags and evidence for it. Choice A states the generalization — some countries' flags carry plant symbols — and then supports it with San Marino's laurel branch. No other option does both jobs.

whyWrong.B: Gives only the single case of San Marino, so there is no generalization, and it adds a claim about national identity that the notes do not make.
whyWrong.C: Defines vexillology and describes what vexillologists study; the symbols themselves never come up.
whyWrong.D: Makes a general statement but supplies no example to support it, and pairs it with the definition of vexillology instead.

tips: For a "make and support a generalization" stem, check that the sentence contains both a broad claim and at least one specific case.

whyCorrect: A difference has to be stated as a comparison, which means both keepers have to appear in the same sentence measured on the same scale. The notes give the scale: Lusby served 1844-1862 and Austin served 1925-1941, so one worked in the nineteenth century and the other in the twentieth. Choice C puts them side by side on exactly that difference.

whyWrong.A: Groups them together as both playing crucial roles, which emphasizes what they share rather than how they differ.
whyWrong.B: Describes Austin alone, so there is nothing to differ from.
whyWrong.D: Describes Lusby alone, and again names only one of the two keepers.

tips: For a difference stem, the correct sentence names both subjects and one property on which they do not match.

whyCorrect: The notes set up an expectation — a capital is usually the largest city — and then give two countries that break it: Manila is the capital while Quezon City is larger, and Vaduz is the capital while Schaan is larger. The similarity is that shared exception, and choice A states it about both countries in one sentence.

whyWrong.B: Names the largest city in each country but never mentions the capitals, so the shared pattern disappears; the "while" framing also makes it read as a contrast.
whyWrong.C: Covers only the Philippines, so no similarity between countries is expressed.
whyWrong.D: Lists the two capitals without saying anything about population, which is the whole basis of the similarity.

commonMistakes: Picking a sentence that mentions both countries without stating what they have in common.

whyCorrect: The first sentence reports critics praising both films, calling one "galvanizing" and the other "picture perfect." The blank is a noun standing in for that praise, and "acclaim" is public praise. It also explains why fans expect new audiences: strong reviews draw viewers.

whyWrong.A: "Ambivalence" is mixed feeling, but the quoted judgments are wholly positive.
whyWrong.C: "Foresight" is the ability to predict what is coming, which has nothing to do with a critic's evaluation of a finished film.
whyWrong.D: "Impartiality" means showing no bias; the critics take a clear positive side, and neutrality would hardly attract new audiences.

tips: When a blank sums up something quoted just before it, match the word to the tone of the quotations.

whyCorrect: "Although" tells you the two halves of the sentence pull in opposite directions. The second half says recent fossil analyses have sharpened our picture, so before that sharpening the picture must have been blurry. "Nebulous" means vague or ill-defined, which is the opposite of sharp.

whyWrong.B: "Intricate" means detailed and complex, which is not the opposite of sharpened — knowledge can be intricate and clear at once.
whyWrong.C: "Unprecedented" means never seen before, a claim about novelty rather than about how clear the knowledge was.
whyWrong.D: "Concrete" means definite and well defined, so it points the same way as "sharpened" and destroys the contrast "although" sets up.

tips: With "although," find the word in the second half that names the change, then choose the opposite of it.

whyCorrect: The comparison is to someone "wakened suddenly from a beautiful dream" who cannot get the dream back. The point of the image is that the waking came without warning and cut the dream off, leaving only a dim trace. "Abruptly" carries exactly that sense of a sharp, unexpected break.

whyWrong.B: "Repeatedly" would mean waking again and again, but the passage describes a single interruption.
whyWrong.C: "Voluntarily" would make the sleeper choose to wake, which removes the involuntary jolt the comparison depends on.
whyWrong.D: "Tenderly" describes a gentle manner, the opposite of the sudden break that leaves the dreamer struggling to recall anything.

commonMistakes: Reading the surrounding words "beautiful" and "dream" as setting a soft tone and choosing a soft-sounding word for the blank.

whyCorrect: The second sentence tells you what the hypotheses are about: the incidence of a word, and specifically that "day" ranks fifth among the most commonly used nouns. That is a claim about how widespread the word is in the language, and "pervasive" means present throughout.

whyWrong.A: "Assertive" describes a forceful manner of speaking, a property of people rather than a measurable feature of a word in a corpus.
whyWrong.B: "Credible" means believable, which applies to a claim, not to how often a word appears.
whyWrong.D: "Profound" means deep or weighty in meaning, which a corpus count cannot measure; the example is about frequency, not significance.

tips: Let the "for instance" sentence define the blank; here it supplies a frequency ranking, so the blank must be about frequency.

whyCorrect: The colon means what follows defines the blank. Sheppard's team has spotted over one hundred satellites while many astronomers are pleased with one or two, so the contrast is purely about quantity. "Plentiful" is the word that describes discoveries in great number.

whyWrong.A: "Inferior" ranks the discoveries as lower in quality, but the comparison flatters the team rather than diminishing it.
whyWrong.B: "Random" describes discoveries made without pattern, which the hundred-versus-two comparison says nothing about.
whyWrong.D: "Likely" means probable, a word about expectation rather than about how many satellites were actually found.

tips: After a colon, look for the numbers or details being contrasted; they tell you which dimension the blank measures.

whyCorrect: Every sentence works toward one point: Carson's album was the first peer-reviewed rap album, its review panel included rap artists rather than only scholars, and it fused mixtape and essay for audiences inside and outside academia. The closing line states the payoff — it helped redefine how scholarship is created and shared. The text exists to lay out what makes that album a break from the norm.

whyWrong.A: No comparison of public impact is made; scholarly articles come up only to explain what ordinary peer review looks like.
whyWrong.B: Peer review is described in a single sentence as background, and its steps are never walked through.
whyWrong.C: The text reports facts about the album rather than any one scholar's opinion of it, and Carson is its creator, not its reviewer.

tips: When a text ends by naming what something changed, the purpose is usually to explain why that thing is significant.

whyCorrect: The first sentence warns that copying one walkable feature of Luang Prabang may not make another city more walkable. The second explains why: Alfonzo argues that research on why people choose to walk is not robust, with different studies stressing different factors and real decisions shaped by many conditions at once. Together they make a point about how hard it is to find a dependable lever for increasing walking anywhere.

whyWrong.A: Human-scaled architecture appears only as an example of a feature that may not transfer, and the text never claims to describe its effect on cities generally.
whyWrong.B: Nothing here is about measuring or comparing traffic volumes; the difficulty concerns causes of walking, not counts of walkers.
whyWrong.C: The text says our understanding of people's decision-making is weak, not that the decision-making itself could be improved.

commonMistakes: Latching onto the architecture example instead of the claim it was introduced to qualify.

whyCorrect: The text names the old belief outright — people thought tool use was unique to primates — and then knocks it down with two non-primate examples, octopuses sheltering in seashell halves and vasa parrots grinding shells with date pits. The main idea is the correction of that belief, and the examples exist only to support it.

whyWrong.A: Ranks octopuses above primates in skill, a comparison the text never makes; octopuses are cited to show tool use is not limited to primates.
whyWrong.B: Widens the point to many myths about tool use when the text addresses exactly one.
whyWrong.C: Contradicts the text, which shows several animals using tools successfully.

tips: When a passage states a former belief and then gives counterexamples, the main idea is the belief being overturned.

whyCorrect: The last sentence gives the general rule for land art: large-scale pieces installed outdoors, often in surprising locations. Ancient Language is an 80-meter geoglyph of rocks in the Atacama Desert and is identified as part of that movement, so the general rule applies to it. That makes its desert setting a location a viewer could well find surprising.

whyWrong.B: The text places the work within an existing movement and says nothing about the movement's popularity rising or falling.
whyWrong.C: Land artists reject the commercialization of galleries, and no claim about commercial success in any location appears.
whyWrong.D: Only the year 2004 is given; nothing indicates where that falls in Rogers's career.

commonMistakes: Treating an inference as free invention; every inference question is answered by applying a general statement in the text to the specific case.

whyCorrect: The text has two moves joined by "however." First, the 'akeke'e, like other Hawaiian birds, is finely adapted to one narrow habitat; second, that very specialization makes it fragile when the ecosystem is disturbed. A main idea has to carry the second half, since that is what the contrast is built toward.

whyWrong.A: Generalizes to all Hawaiian birds and stops at specialization, dropping the vulnerability that the "however" sentence exists to deliver.
whyWrong.C: Claims the 'akeke'e shares its habitat with no other bird, which the text never says; "like many other bird species" points the other way.
whyWrong.D: Reports the specialization and the relation to other species but leaves out the consequence, so it summarizes only the setup.

tips: When a short text turns on "however," the main idea lives on the far side of that turn.

whyCorrect: The finding is a comparison between two hardening types: bulkheads drag community integrity down more than riprap does. Supporting it requires a site dominated by bulkheads to score lower on the IWCI than a site dominated by riprap, which is exactly what a lower average at Old Road than at Miles gives you.

whyWrong.A: Compares two bulkhead-heavy sites with each other and reports no significant difference, so it never sets bulkheads against riprap.
whyWrong.B: Compares a site with equal shares of the two structures against a site with unequal shares, which cannot isolate which structure is worse.
whyWrong.D: Compares heavily hardened shoreline against lightly hardened shoreline, supporting the idea that hardening in general lowers integrity but saying nothing about bulkheads versus riprap.

tips: A finding stated as a comparison needs evidence that varies exactly the thing being compared and holds the rest steady.

whyCorrect: The claim names two things to illustrate: Jim's energy and his absorption in play so complete that he is distracted from what is around him. The quotation about Jim being "engine Number 36," running behind time with "the throttle was wide open," shows both — the wide-open throttle is the energy, and the fact that he has become a locomotive in his own mind is the absorption.

whyWrong.A: Shows Jim after the accident, trying to prop the damaged peony back up, which is attention to consequences rather than absorbed play.
whyWrong.B: Shows him hanging back and confessing to his father, illustrating reluctance, not energetic distraction.
whyWrong.D: Describes the father mowing with his back turned; Jim does not appear in it at all.

tips: Match every element of the claim; a quotation that captures only the aftermath cannot illustrate the state of mind that caused it.

whyCorrect: The claim is about change over the course of Bonheur's development, so the supporting quotation has to contrast her work before The Horse Fair with her work after it. Saying that everything painted earlier belongs to a style she never returned to marks the painting as the dividing line, which is precisely a significant change.

whyWrong.B: Ranks The Horse Fair as her best representation of her abilities, which is a judgment of quality, not evidence that her work changed at that point.
whyWrong.C: Concerns disagreement among viewers over the painting's meaning, which is about interpretation rather than about her artistic development.
whyWrong.D: Places her relative to other artists of her time; influence and being ahead of her time say nothing about a shift within her own body of work.

commonMistakes: Choosing the most flattering statement about the painting instead of the one that addresses change over time.

whyCorrect: Sort the products by type first. Induction cookers use ferritic steel; washing machines use the 200 series and furnaces the 300 series, and both series are austenitic. Ferritic is the type with at least 10.5% chromium, more than austenitic has, so both austenitic products fall below that 10.5% mark — and furnaces and washing machines are both austenitic.

whyWrong.B: Reverses the nickel comparison. Furnaces use the 300 series, which the text says has more nickel than the 200 series used for washing machines.
whyWrong.C: Assigns the face-centered cubic structure to induction cookers, but the text says that structure belongs to austenitic steel, and it opens that sentence with "Unlike ferritic stainless steel."
whyWrong.D: Nitrogen is named only as a stabilizer in austenitic steel; nothing in the text lets you claim ferritic induction-cooker steel has a similar amount.

tips: On a classification inference, label every product with its category before you read the choices; most distractors just swap two labels.

whyCorrect: Line the dates up. Swords were not made in Britain until the Middle Bronze Age, roughly the 14th to 10th centuries BCE. The Llanarmon-yn-Ial hoard holds 16th-century BCE artifacts, from before swords existed, while the Horsehope Craig hoard holds 7th-century BCE artifacts, from well after. So the sword evidence appears in Horsehope Craig and is absent from Llanarmon-yn-Ial.

whyWrong.A: Puts sword evidence in both hoards, but the older hoard predates the invention of swords in Britain entirely.
whyWrong.B: Sorts the hoards by the years they were dug up, 1865 and 1982, when the explanation depends on the age of the artifacts, not on excavation dates.
whyWrong.C: Contrasts sword production with intact swords inside the older hoard, which still credits that hoard with sword production it could not have had.

commonMistakes: Mixing up the excavation year with the artifacts' date; the text deliberately makes the older hoard the one found more recently.

whyCorrect: Two decisions sit in this blank. "Lawmakers" is a plain plural doing the designating, so it takes no apostrophe. "The state's official fossil" does show ownership — the fossil belongs to the state — so that noun takes a singular possessive apostrophe.

whyWrong.B: Gets "lawmakers" right but writes "the states official fossil," leaving the possessive unmarked so the phrase reads as a plural noun with no owner.
whyWrong.C: Marks the subject as possessive, which would mean the fossil designated something belonging to a lawmaker, and drops the needed apostrophe on "state's."
whyWrong.D: Correctly writes "the state's" but turns the subject into "lawmaker's," which is a possessive, not a plural subject for "designated."

tips: Handle each noun in the blank separately; these items almost always test one plural and one possessive in the same sentence.

whyCorrect: The subject is "The dedication," a singular noun; "of Greely and her fellow activists" is a prepositional phrase telling you whose dedication it was, and phrases like that never determine the verb. The rewarding happened in 1920, a finished moment in the past, so the verb is the singular past "was."

whyWrong.B: Plural, and the present perfect conflicts with the specific past date 1920.
whyWrong.C: Plural and present tense, so it disagrees with the subject and with the 1920 time frame.
whyWrong.D: Past tense but plural, chosen by agreeing with "activists" rather than with "dedication."

commonMistakes: Hearing the plural noun just before the blank and matching the verb to it.

whyCorrect: "They are hardly pristine, though" is a complete sentence, and "many chondrites experience aqueous alteration ... due to collisions with other objects" is another. "Though" here is an adverb attached to the first clause, set off by a comma, and the semicolon then does the real work of separating the two independent clauses.

whyWrong.B: Moving "though" past the semicolon turns the second half into a subordinate clause, so the sentence after the semicolon has no main clause and becomes a fragment.
whyWrong.C: Leaves only a comma between two independent clauses, which is a comma splice.
whyWrong.D: Also joins the two clauses with a comma; the extra comma after "though" does not change that it is still a splice.

tips: Decide which clause the stray adverb belongs to first; once "though" is parked in the first clause, you can see that a semicolon is needed after it.

whyCorrect: "Confiscated from the private collections of French aristocrats" is a single prepositional phrase, and "from" needs its object attached to it. Nothing is being joined, separated, or introduced, so no punctuation belongs between the preposition and the noun phrase it governs.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and "the private collections of French aristocrats" is not a clause.
whyWrong.C: A colon needs a complete statement before it, but "It was filled with living animals that had been confiscated from" is left hanging.
whyWrong.D: A comma here cuts the preposition off from its object, breaking a phrase that has to stay together.

tips: Never punctuate between a preposition and its object; if the words on both sides of the blank form one phrase, leave it alone.

whyCorrect: The sentence lists three languages, and each item already contains internal commas: COBOL, developed by Grace Hopper in 1959; Java, developed by James Gosling in 1995; and Clojure, developed by Rich Hickey in 2007. When items carry their own commas, the items are separated by semicolons, and the comma inside each item stays put to set off the descriptive phrase.

whyWrong.A: Mixes the two systems, using a comma between the first and second items and a semicolon before the third, and it drops the comma that should set off Java's description.
whyWrong.B: Puts a semicolon inside the second item, cutting "Java" off from the phrase describing it.
whyWrong.C: Uses a semicolon after the first item but a comma before "and Clojure," so the separators are inconsistent and the boundary between items disappears.

tips: If any list item contains a comma, every item boundary in that list becomes a semicolon.

whyCorrect: The phrase "to this day" pins the verb to the present, and the sentence contrasts what modern chemists commonly use with ancient emulsifiers that chemists still use now. The subject "emulsifiers ... such as beeswax and egg yolk" is plural, so the present-tense plural "are" is what fits.

whyWrong.A: "Would have been" describes a hypothetical past outcome, which clashes with a statement about current practice.
whyWrong.B: Simple past says the use stopped, contradicting "to this day."
whyWrong.C: "Were being" places the use in the past and in progress, again incompatible with the present time frame.

tips: Look for a time marker like "to this day" or "currently" before choosing a tense; it usually settles the question by itself.

whyCorrect: Read the tail of the sentence first: whatever fills the blank has to be the thing that resulted in the dances being received as groundbreaking artworks rather than as mere experiments. A radical departure alone would explain the "experimental" half; what turns experiment into art is execution, so the added point about skill and artistry supplies the missing cause, and "moreover" marks it as an addition to the radical-departure claim.

whyWrong.B: Being a dancer as well as a choreographer is a fact about his training, and it neither specifies the previous sentence nor explains how the works were received.
whyWrong.C: Founding a company in 1953 is an event, not a quality of the work, so it cannot be why the pieces were judged groundbreaking artworks.
whyWrong.D: "In contrast" contradicts the previous sentence rather than building on it, and a reputation as an unpredictable iconoclast supports the "experimental spectacle" reading the sentence is arguing against.

tips: When the choices are whole clauses, test the logic of the clause first and the transition word second.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says most trompe l'oeil paintings fool the eye with quotidian objects — a fly, an empty cage. Van Houbraken's painting instead delivers an "extraordinary sight" of a man leaning out of the frame. Ordinary versus extraordinary is a direct opposition, so the blank needs a contrast transition.

whyWrong.A: "Fittingly" would say the painting matches the pattern just described, but it departs from it.
whyWrong.C: "For instance" makes the painting an example of using everyday objects, which is exactly what it is not.
whyWrong.D: "Specifically" narrows the previous claim to a detail, and a man's head emerging from the frame is not a detail of the quotidian-object technique.

commonMistakes: Assuming any single painting named after a general claim must be an example of it; check whether it fits the claim or breaks it.

whyCorrect: The second sentence defines the rule: the seat goes to whoever has the most votes, not to whoever has more than half. The third sentence spells out what that rule makes possible when several popular candidates split the vote — a winner under 50%. That is a consequence drawn from the definition, so the blank takes a result transition.

whyWrong.A: "However" signals a contradiction, but winning with under 50% follows directly from a plurality rule instead of conflicting with it.
whyWrong.B: "Moreover" adds a separate point, hiding that the third sentence is derived from the second.
whyWrong.D: "Similarly" implies a parallel case, and only one voting system is under discussion.

tips: If the sentence after the blank could start with "so" or "therefore," you need a result transition.

whyCorrect: The notes contain one point on which the two plants match and several on which they differ. They match in botanical classification: both strawberries and green beans are fruits. Choice B states that shared classification for both plants in a single sentence, which is what emphasizing a similarity requires.

whyWrong.A: Opens with "Unlike" and reports the difference in taste, so it emphasizes what separates them.
whyWrong.C: Contrasts how each is commonly regarded, fruit versus vegetable, which is again a difference.
whyWrong.D: Discusses strawberries only, so there is no comparison of any kind.

tips: Scan the notes for the one fact stated about both items in the same terms; that is almost always the similarity being tested.

whyCorrect: The evidence lies in a mismatch between two facts, and the sentence has to hold both. The pendulum's swing path never actually changes because it hangs from a fixed point, yet an observer sees the path shift over time — and the only way to explain that is that the ground beneath it is turning. Choice C states the unchanging path, the apparent change, and the rotation that reconciles them.

whyWrong.A: Gives the fixed path and the rotating Earth but omits the apparent change an observer sees, so the sentence never explains what anyone actually observes as evidence.
whyWrong.B: Describes the pendulum's parts and asserts that it provides evidence without explaining how it does so.
whyWrong.D: Only locates a pendulum in Oslo and repeats the claim; no mechanism is given at all.

tips: A "how" or "why" stem needs a sentence containing a because or a contrast, not just the claim being explained.

whyCorrect: The goal is narrow: state the American paddlefish's chromosome count. The notes give it as 120, and choice C reports exactly that number for exactly that fish. Nothing further is required, and extra material would only dilute the specification.

whyWrong.A: Explains what chromosomes do without ever giving a count.
whyWrong.B: Says the paddlefish has more than the carp, which is a relative comparison rather than the specific number the stem asks for.
whyWrong.D: Gives a count, but for the crucian carp, not for the American paddlefish.

commonMistakes: Passing over the shortest option because it looks too plain; when the stem asks for one fact, the sentence that states just that fact is correct.

whyCorrect: The sentence calls Al-Sweedan and Alhaj's below-sea-level focus "the novel path," and "though" sets their work against the many studies described in the blank. If theirs is the new approach, the earlier studies are the customary one, so the blank needs a word meaning long-established.

whyWrong.A: "Eccentric" means odd or unconventional, which would make the earlier studies the unusual ones and leave the new study with nothing to depart from.
whyWrong.C: "Meager" comments on how thin the research was, but the contrast is about which approach is usual, not about quality or quantity.
whyWrong.D: "Random" describes studies chosen without system, which neither contrasts with novelty nor fits a body of research on a defined question.

tips: When one side of a contrast is labeled new or novel, the other side is conventional, not merely different.

whyCorrect: The blank is governed by "therefore," so it must follow from what comes before: the mihrab is one of the features foundational to traditional mosque architecture. A feature that is foundational is the most representative example of the type, which is what "quintessential" means.

whyWrong.A: "Imposing" describes size or grandeur, which does not follow from being foundational to a tradition.
whyWrong.B: "Embellished" describes decoration added to something, a claim about ornament rather than about how central the feature is.
whyWrong.D: "Unprecedented" means without any earlier example, the opposite of a feature that has anchored the tradition all along.

tips: A "therefore" before the blank means the answer has to be a restatement of the reason just given.

whyCorrect: The opening phrase gives the cause — widely celebrated portraits of prominent figures — and the blank names what those portraits produced for Edwards. Prestige is something an artist gains through such work, so the verb has to mean earned or gained.

whyWrong.A: "Required" would mean the prestige was a precondition of his work rather than its result, reversing the cause and effect the sentence sets up.
whyWrong.B: "Remembered" takes a memory as its object; prestige is not something a person recalls.
whyWrong.D: "Avoided" contradicts "widely celebrated," which shows the recognition landed on him rather than being escaped.

tips: Check that the verb runs in the same direction as the cause stated at the front of the sentence.

whyCorrect: The colon explains the blank, and what follows is about links running from present-day writers back to the traditional stories of the Kanaka Maoli. A thread that persists from older tradition into current work is thematic continuity, and "although" confirms the blank must oppose the heterogeneity mentioned first.

whyWrong.A: "Innovation" is about breaking from what came before, but the evidence after the colon is about connections to older stories.
whyWrong.C: "Subtlety" describes how delicately themes are handled, which the scholars' connections do not measure.
whyWrong.D: "Sophistication" judges the literature's refinement and would not be demonstrated by tracing links to traditional narratives.

tips: Whatever follows a colon defines the blank; read it before you look at the options.

whyCorrect: After the colon the delta is described as "constantly evolving," with channels and strips of land that "change in size and shape" as new sediment arrives. The blank must sum up that ongoing change, and "mutable" means liable to change.

whyWrong.B: "Habitable" concerns whether the delta can support living there, a question the description never raises.
whyWrong.C: "Secluded" is about isolation from other places, but the passage describes the delta's internal shifting, not its remoteness.
whyWrong.D: "Homogeneous" means uniform throughout, which conflicts with a network of channels and land strips that keep changing size and shape.

tips: When a colon supplies a definition, pick the word that is the shortest summary of that definition.

whyCorrect: The two references appear in a list of what different studies emphasize, and that list is offered as proof that our understanding is "insufficiently robust." The sentence then ends by saying walking decisions are made in complex contexts where multiple conditions and needs matter. So each named factor is a real influence that some research has singled out, but only one of many at work — which is why copying a single feature of another city may not increase walking.

whyWrong.A: Nothing restricts these factors to Zurich; Zurich is the city whose feature might not transfer, not a place with unique decision factors.
whyWrong.B: The text never claims people rarely consider these factors; it claims no single factor accounts for the decision on its own.
whyWrong.D: Alfonzo's point is that understanding is incomplete, not that these particular factors have been overemphasized.

tips: For a function question, ask what the surrounding argument is using the detail to prove, not whether the detail itself is true.

whyCorrect: Follow the shape sentence by sentence. The first two establish a trend: customization is spreading and shoppers help design what they buy. The third gives the upside for companies, since customers pay more and wait longer. The final sentence, opening with "Still," gives the downside, since mass production cannot easily make a one-off item cheaply. Trend, then benefit, then challenge.

whyWrong.A: No manufacturing innovations are named, and no future applications are proposed; the text stays on a market trend and its consequences.
whyWrong.B: No specific company or its recent success appears; the discussion is about companies in general.
whyWrong.C: Only one technique, customization, is discussed, so there is no pair of contrasting techniques.

tips: Structure questions are settled by the connective words; "in turn" and "still" mark the benefit and the challenge here.

whyCorrect: The final sentence reports two findings, and each one links a factor to behavior. White butterflies were seen on green flowers more often than other butterflies were, which ties color to where they perch and feed. Butterflies fed more often on cloudy days, which ties weather to feeding. Both factors are therefore linked to behavior.

whyWrong.A: Drops the color finding, even though the white-butterfly result is stated as its own observation about behavior.
whyWrong.B: Drops the weather finding, though the cloudy-day feeding result is stated just as directly.
whyWrong.C: Denies both findings, which the sentence reports explicitly.

tips: When the stem asks which factors were linked, count the findings; each separate clause after "found that" usually contributes one.

whyCorrect: The last sentence says historians of capitalism lean on longitudinal economic data from archival records, and that such records largely do not exist for precolonial Africa. Yet Iliffe and other Africanist scholars have demonstrated that private land ownership and salaried labor were present there. They could not have shown that from records that do not exist, so they must be drawing on other kinds of evidence.

whyWrong.B: Both groups treat the same things as capitalist features; the disagreement is about whether those features were present in precolonial Africa, not about what counts.
whyWrong.C: You cannot derive data from archives that do not exist, so a difference in method applied to those same records is not what the text implies.
whyWrong.D: The text never addresses whether capitalism benefited Africa; it addresses when capitalism appeared there.

commonMistakes: Reading the final sentence as describing both groups; it describes only the historians of capitalism and thereby implies the contrast.

whyCorrect: The claim has two parts, and the quotation must satisfy both: Winnemucca has to speak to the reader directly and has to explain a custom. "Now, my dear reader" is the direct address, and "that is why my people call all good people father or mother" explains the custom of using those terms of kinship.

whyWrong.B: Explains the custom of naming girls after flowers but never turns to the reader; it stays inside the narrative.
whyWrong.C: Recounts family history with no address to the reader and no explanation of a custom.
whyWrong.D: Addresses the reader as "dear readers" but explains nothing; it declines to describe the scene.

tips: When a claim names two features, discard any quotation that satisfies only one of them, however well it does so.

whyCorrect: The hypothesis is specific: the foliage gleaner, M. guttata, whose field of vision is limited while foraging, should be more sensitive to warning signals from neighboring species than the sallying M. fusca, which can watch for predators as it hunts. Supporting it means playing an alarm call from a species that shares their territory and seeing the gleaner react while the sallier does not, which is exactly what this finding reports.

whyWrong.A: Has M. guttata reacting to meaningless control noise, which suggests indiscriminate skittishness rather than sensitivity to warning signals, and it has both species reacting to the real alarm calls, erasing the predicted difference.
whyWrong.B: Uses calls from a species that does not share their territory, so it does not test sensitivity to neighboring species, and the reaction comes from the wrong bird.
whyWrong.D: Uses the two species' own alarm calls rather than a neighboring species', so it tests response to conspecifics instead of the hypothesis's claim.

tips: Check the control in each option; a result that appears with random noise cannot show sensitivity to a signal.

whyCorrect: The claim is that The Horse Fair marks a significant change in Bonheur's development, so the useful quotation is the one that divides her career at that painting. Saying everything before it belongs to an earlier style she never went back to establishes exactly that break.

whyWrong.B: Calls it her most representative work, which praises the painting without showing that her work changed after it.
whyWrong.C: Reports disagreement among viewers over its meaning, which concerns interpretation rather than the artist's development.
whyWrong.D: Places her among the artists of her era and calls her ahead of her time, saying nothing about a shift within her own career.

commonMistakes: Treating any strong praise of the painting as support; the claim is about change over time, so the evidence must compare before and after.

whyCorrect: Translate each grain type into an environment. Most of the sediment is fine mudstone that settles out of suspension in low-flow water, which means standing water like a lake persisted for a long time. Those fine grains show cracks from episodic desiccation, so the lake dried out now and then. The scattered intervals of coarse sandstone mean flowing water, that is, streams, at some periods. A long-lived lake that occasionally dried, with streams at intervals, is the only reading that uses all three facts.

whyWrong.B: Denies that the lake dried, but the desiccation cracks appear in the fine grains, which are the lake deposits themselves.
whyWrong.C: Reverses the proportions. Mudstone dominates the formation, so the lake was the long-lived feature, not a brief episode that ended in permanent drying.
whyWrong.D: Rules out a lake entirely, which contradicts the finding that most of the sediment formed by slow settling in low-flow water.

tips: Map every piece of evidence to a condition before reading the options, then reject any option that leaves one piece unexplained.

whyCorrect: Chain the three facts. Most of these at-risk plants depend on birds eating their fruit and carrying the seeds elsewhere; every native fruit-eating bird on Oahu is extinct; and studies confirm the introduced birds are now doing the seed spreading. If the only remaining seed dispersers are the non-native birds, those birds may now be necessary for the plants to survive.

whyWrong.A: Compares present numbers with what native birds once did, but the text gives no figures for either period.
whyWrong.B: Claims a preference for native fruit over non-native fruit, which no part of the text measures.
whyWrong.D: Speculates about other activities affecting the plants, while the text supports a conclusion about the seed dispersal it actually documents.

tips: An inference should use the facts given and add nothing; discard any option that requires a comparison or a preference the text never mentions.

whyCorrect: The sentence already has its main verb: the codes "later changed." What the blank needs is a modifier telling you where those codes came from, and the past participle does that job — "the codes assigned by the Committee later changed." Any option with a full verb would give the sentence two predicates and no way to join them.

whyWrong.B: "Would be assigned" is a complete verb, so the sentence runs "Most codes would be assigned ... later changed," with two finite verbs and no conjunction.
whyWrong.C: "Had been assigned" is likewise a full verb and produces the same collision with "changed."
whyWrong.D: "Were assigned" reads naturally until you reach "changed," at which point the sentence has two main verbs stacked with nothing linking them.

tips: Scan for the main verb before filling a blank like this; if the sentence already has one, the blank almost certainly wants a participle.

whyCorrect: "Fulfilling one of the criteria required for a species to be considered endangered" has no subject and no finite verb, so it is a participial phrase commenting on the whole clause before it. That kind of trailing modifier attaches with a comma.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon must have an independent clause on both sides, and the material after the blank is a phrase.
whyWrong.B: A colon introduces a list, a definition, or an explanatory statement; a participial phrase describing what the population figure amounts to is not the kind of element a colon takes.
whyWrong.C: A period leaves "Fulfilling one of the criteria ..." standing alone as a sentence fragment.

tips: An -ing phrase that comments on the whole preceding clause is joined with a comma, never with a semicolon or period.

whyCorrect: Look at what follows the blank: "a theoretical relationship between tax rates and revenues, the curve was famously sketched on a napkin by economist Arthur Laffer in 1974." That is a complete clause with its own subject and verb, opened by an appositive phrase describing the curve. The words before the blank are also a complete clause, so the two need a semicolon between them.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation the two clauses fuse into a run-on.
whyWrong.C: "Which is" turns the description into a relative clause attached to the first sentence, but "the curve was famously sketched" then follows with nothing joining it, leaving a splice.
whyWrong.D: A comma makes the description an appositive on the first clause and still leaves the second clause spliced on after it.

tips: Read past the blank to the end of the sentence; a second subject-verb pair means a boundary is required, not just a pause.

whyCorrect: The words after the blank already form a complete sentence: "they take a bit of sand home, though, it disturbs the beach's ecosystem" needs "When" attached to the first half so it reads "When they take a bit of sand home, though, it disturbs the beach's ecosystem." That leaves "... an unusual orange tint that dazzles visitors" as its own complete sentence, so a period is what belongs in the blank.

whyWrong.A: Puts a comma where a sentence boundary is needed, so the dazzling clause and the disturbing clause end up spliced together.
whyWrong.B: "And when" subordinates the second half to the first, but "it disturbs the beach's ecosystem" is then left as a main clause with no conjunction of its own.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation at all, "dazzles visitors when they take a bit of sand home" wrongly says the sand dazzles only while being taken, and the rest of the sentence still runs on.

tips: Locate the subordinating word and decide which clause it opens; that usually shows you where the sentence boundary has to fall.
